I am studying at a STEM university and went to a mediocre high school so I was never school taught (discussed and thoroughly reviewed) a lot of philosophical texts. Specifically I am looking for a good textbook on Plato's Republic but all other recommendations are welcome. Thank you for your time

I can't help you with a specific textbook, but I can point you to https://www.partiallyexaminedlife.com/. Their podcasts are usually based on a philosophical text and provide an easy to understand background for those of us who find diving into http://plato.stanford.edu/ a bit dry at times.

Here is the link to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's article on the Republic: http://plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato-ethics-politics/

Here is the link to The Partially Examined Life's podcast on the Republic: http://www.partiallyexaminedlife.com/2011/07/11/episode-40-platos-republic-what-is-justice/

Hope this helps.
Not OP but thanks. I am slowly easing my way into logic and philosophy. I think this will help.

How I have read the majority of classical texts, and really all texts available that are in the public domain, is through Project Gutenberg and Librivox. For those of us with jobs that consume 8 hours of our days against our will to learn, this and podcasts can give us 8 hours of continuous learning and reflection. If I may additionally remark, the reading of "Apology" on Librivox, by "Bob Neufeld" is a great listen. The down side is, of course, some of the volunteer readers are utterly incompetent elocutors.

Through gutenberg you get access to public domain translations, and on the internet access to commentaries as well as further learning. Through these not only do you have audio access to histories (including Histories by Herodotus), public domain multi-volume historical works, and others relevant to philosophy.

If you are capable of doing it as I have, you can actually say to have read more or less every foundational work of philosophy generally available, in approximately a single year. Comprehension and commentary require additional learning, but commentaries are also available in audio form. I think it's helpful in learning the process of reason in philosophy, and incredibly helpful in learning of the many ways in which biased reason leads one astray. It's entirely up to you if you think certain works (like Montaigne) would ever be worth its essay rambling.

One last note. Foundational works are very different from the current goings on in philosophy, although terminology and logic may be famous or referenced quite often. Never assume, as some mistakenly do, that the works of Kant or Nietzsche are the last thing said about the philosophy involved in their respective works.
Thank you. Not OP, but this helps a lot.

For Plato's republic, try Allan Bloom's translation. I can read ancient Greek (with some difficulty) and Bloom's translation is pretty accurate, but translation is much more an art than a science, especially with ancient Greek. He certainly manages to capture the spirit of what was being discussed while presenting in an accessible manner to the modern reader.

 

After The Republic, I would recommend that you move on to the other Platonic dialogues and/or Aristotle's Nichomachean Ethics. I can't recommend Aristotle enough. Where you go from there is up to you, but most philosophy professors will move to the Germans (Kant and Hegel specifically), however, I recommend that you give Confucius and Mencius a read. Their style and presentation is very different from the ancient Greeks, but they are very easy to grasp and they manage to say incredibly profound things in an enjoyable manner. The reason I recommend the Ancient Chinese right after the ancient Greeks isn't just because the cultures are so different, but because they actually have a lot in common. There are many parallels between Aristotle and the Confucian tradition, and they play off of each other well; one revealing different insights and truths in the other.

Bloom's translation was my first introduction to philosophy and I couldnt agree more with this suggestion. His interpretation was highly influential in developing what has become a life long pursuit.

Bloom includes an essay in the back that can be read along with the translated text that's incredibly helpful in understanding, not just the arguments put forth in the text, but also the tone and perspective of the individual participants.
Was it a professor that introduced you to Allan Bloom, or did you discover him on your own?

It was a professor. Bloom's translation is amazing on its own, but the professor pulled everything out of that text he could and really made it digestible.
